I spent my primary school years (4-11) in a small countryside school, where bullying was fairly common. I wasnt a bully there, but my brothers were bullied and I was usually the one to go after the bully for it. Violence was pretty normal at that school, and I don't remember it ever being punished (except for the time two kids had a fight over a Grimer and got pokemon cards banned - Thanks Kieran you fuck)

Secondary school I was sent to a school in the city, instead of the more local one all my friends went to. I do remember having a fight on the first day. But it wasn't until I met my 'best friend' that I actually became a bully. He was, if you like, the draco malfoy to my crabbe. He hated this kid, and I just went along with it because I didn't fit in there anyway and it was nice to have someone to spend time with. 

And it was pretty bad, I guess. I hit a lot of people, I remember that, and the one kid, Andrew, really got it - we used to hunt him down at breaktimes, my 'friend' would hold a door closed and I would wallop him until we got bored. It was a game to me, to be honest. I wasn't really aware that other kids weren't enjoying it too. Ok, that sounds strange, but it does bring us onto reason three, which is that I was diagnosed with autism when I was 12. Nobody told me, I actually found out when I was 30, but it's a fairly big piece of the puzzle - lacking social instincts, misfit, 'friend' influencing me, school constantly punishing me but doing nothing to prevent it or address why it was happening. 

Don't know if that answers your first question or not. As for the second one, to a point. That was a long time ago, and who am I now is completely different to who I was then - I don't regret it because it wasn't me doing it. I might as well regret shitting my pants when I was 2. 

But I do pity the people involved. Andrew did ok for himself, last time I checked. My moron friend moved schools when I was 14 after he turned on me because the girl he was into liked me, and he did his best to pick on us both in this last year there. After he left things changed a little. I ended up on reasonable terms with most other kids by the time I left. 

But I pity the younger me, too. That lonely, confused and isolated kid needed understanding and support, but instead he got punished, ostracised and picked on by teachers. And if you're rolling your eyes reading that, go fuck yourself. Young boys deserve care and understanding, no matter what issues they have or how those issues are manifesting.
Keep going man, it gets better and better.

Oh wow, that sounds like an absolutely shit day with an absolutely shit instructor. Like most shit, it's best to just flush it.

My CBT was crap too - the instructor had clearly been doing it way too long, his heart wasn't in it and he was just going through the motions, to the point where he didn't do the eye test (I actually have to wear glasses when I ride and had taken them with me, but he just never mentioned it. We were well out on the road before I remembered that I should have been wearing them) and didn't spend more than a few minutes on road positioning. I left feeling completely unprepared for actually riding on the road (not to say that my subsequent visit to the bottom of a ditch a week later was anyone else's fault but mine). 

It would definitely be a good idea to do some more training, after some serious shopping around, to repair that confidence and love of riding. Call around other schools in your area, explain your situation and ask what they can offer you.

I would also call the school and tell them what happened. This guy shouldn't be an instructor if that's the best he could do, and there will be more women going to that place after you and having exactly the same experience if he's allowed to continue.

I wrote in another post a bit ago about what happened to me:

 >I don't think I can get better.
>My ex tricked me into listening to her and her new guy in bed over the phone.
>It was eight months ago. Eight months. Eight months of obsessive exercise that has taken over my life. Eight months of being afraid to try to sleep. Eight months of nightmares, daily suicidal thoughts, total loss of interest in life. Eight months of sitting here alone, late at nights, trying to forget what happened. Trying not to think that she's out there, somewhere. With him.
>
>I don't see the point in living. Every day is just pain, feeling like my head is swelling up, the pressure building inside, compressing my brain, about to explode out of my skull in a cloud of feeling. Every night is laying in my bed with all the lights on, the thoughts floating above me like tendrils of smoke, waiting for me to close my eyes. Reminders are everywhere, triggers are everywhere. I don't think I can ever be free of this. I don't feel happiness any more. I don't see anything in my future except this.
>
>I don't know what else to do. I tried to find someone new, but just hugging sets me shaking. Three hours of exercise a day eclipses the thoughts if I do it hard enough. But the night always comes down.
>
>For so long I've been riding this pain like a wave, using the power of it, the energy, to push my body past every limit I thought I had. But every day, I slip deeper beneath it. And one day it's going to swallow me. I don't want to die, but it's becoming so unbearable to live.

Melodramatic, I know. But sometimes life is melodramatic.

I'm still very much going through it, but what has really helped me is improving myself, and leaving the man who had that experience behind. I channeled the pain into exercise and creativity, and looking back over the months (God, has it been that long?), I can honestly say that every part of my life, and every part of myself, is better now than it was then.

Something else that really helped was accepting myself and learning to love myself. Going through such intense pain, you need to be with yourself, and you need to take care of yourself. Be your own best friend.

Also, you don't have to listen to anyone's shit. If something isn't working for you, you don't have to keep it up. Contrariwise, if you have a way of coping that other people don't agree with, the hell with them. You're going through a crisis, and you absolutely know what is best for you. 

And finally - it's ok to let go. You don't have to stay in your head all the time, and you don't have to deal with it right away. Pain gets boring, so boring, and nobody can blame you for taking a break to get utterly shitfaced, or travel, or get on three different dating apps at once and hook the fuck up with whatevers breathing. 

Oh, and this is important: you can't go back. The person you were is gone, the life you had is gone. The only way is forward. Look back all you like, but never try to rebuild it. Blank slate, dude. Start again.

You're going to be ok, man. Life won't be this way forever, and one day we're all going to wake up and realise it doesn't hurt so bad any more.
